label: thm: mainthm2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: mainthm2} Let $d\in {\mathbb N}$ with $d\geq 3$ and $Q>\frac{d(d-1)+2}{2}$. There exists a PI manifold $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d},\mu)$ that satisfies:
\begin{enumerate} 
                                                     
\item $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d})$ is a linearly locally contractible complete geodesic metric space, whose distance induces the standard topology of ${\mathbb R}^d$,
\item every weak tangent of $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d})$ is homeomorphic to ${\mathbb R}^d$,
\item $\mu$ is equal to a multiple of the Lebesgue measure on ${\mathbb R}^d$,
\item $\mu$ is doubling, 
\item the space satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality,
\item the space has analytic dimension $2$, and
\item the space has $\mu$-essential Hausdorff dimension $Q$ and every set of positive measure has Hausdorff dimension at least $Q$.
\end{enumerate}

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: oscillationversion}
Given $d\in {\mathbb N}$ with $d\geq 3$ and a continuous function $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$, let 
$({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_f,\lambda)$ be the metric measure space, where $\mathbf{d}_f$ is defined in \eqref{eq:metricdef} via the vector fields \eqref{eq:vectdef}, and $\lambda$ is the Lebesgue measure.
If $f $ has doubling oscillation, then 
$({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_f,\lambda)$ is complete, geodesic, homeomorphic to Euclidean space, LLC and doubling, and there exists a constant $C>1$ such that 
\[
C^{-1}r^d \rho^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}}\leq \lambda(B(\mathbf{p},r))\leq C r^d \rho^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}}, \qquad \forall\mathbf{p}\in {\mathbb R}^d \ \  \forall r>0,
\]
with $\rho=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r])$, where $p_1$ is the first component of $\mathbf{p}$.
If moreover $f$ has reverse doubling oscillation, then $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_f,\lambda)$ also satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality.
                                                               
                                                                                                                                  
The constants are controlled by the dimension $d$ and the doubling and reverse doubling constants of $f$.

label: d_X rectifiability
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d_X rectifiability}
Consider a continuous Carnot-Carathéodory structure $(M,\Delta,\|\cdot\|)$.
Let $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ be a curve in $M$ that has finite length with respect to the CC metric $d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}$. Then, the reparametrization of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ by
arc length is $\Delta$-horizontal.
Moreover, for every $\Delta$-horizontal curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$, the length with respect to $d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}$ equals $ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The statement is local in nature. We can therefore think that $M$ is a neighbourhood of ${\bf 0}$ in ${\mathbb R}^d$ and, by scaling the norm, we may assume that $d$ is greater than the Euclidean distance $d_E$.
 Consequently, if $\boldsymbol{\gamma}: I\to {\mathbb R}^d$ is parametrized by
arc length with respect to the length of $d:=d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}$, we have 
$$d_E(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(s),\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\leq d (\boldsymbol{\gamma}(s),\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\leq {\rm L}_d(\boldsymbol{\gamma}|^{t}_{s})=\left|t-s\right|,\qquad \forall s,t\in I.$$
In other words, the curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is (Euclidean) Lipschitz, so absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere, by Rademacher's theorem.

Let $t$ be a point of differentiability. Without loss of generality, we assume $t=0, \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)={\bf 0},$ $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)$ exists and \begin{equation}\label{ipotesi Delta}
 \Delta_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)}={\mathbb R}^k\times\{0\}^{d-k}\subseteq {\mathbb R}^d. 
\end{equation}
So, to prove that $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$
                                               
is horizontal at $t=0$, we need to show that $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)
\in {\mathbb R}^k\times\{0\}^{d-k}$.
                        
Suppose, by way of contradiction, that this is not the case, then, up to reindexing the variables, we have that the last component $\dot\gamma_d(0)$ of $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)$ is not 0. 
                                      
                                                                 
                                                                         
                                   
                       
               
                                                                                                              
                                        
Without loss of generality, there is $c>0$ such that $\dot\gamma_d(0)=2c>0$.
From this we can assume that 
\begin{equation}\label{stima}
\gamma_d(t)>ct,\qquad \text{for all small enough } t>0.
\end{equation} 

Let $X_1,\ldots, X_k$ be pointwise linearly independent, continuous vector fields that define 
$\Delta$, as in \eqref{def Delta vectors}. Up to a biLipschitz change of the metric, we can assume that the norm $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm, and that the vector fields $X_1,\ldots, X_k$ are orthonormal.
                                                                                            

By the assumption \eqref{ipotesi Delta}, for each $\varepsilon >0$, choose $r=r_\varepsilon$ such that on the Euclidean ball we have
                                                                                      
\begin{equation}\label{X2 minore di eps}
|(X_j(p))_d|<\varepsilon, \qquad \forall p\in B_E({\bf 0} , r), \forall j\in \{1, \ldots, k\},
\end{equation}
where $(X)_d$ denotes the $d$'th component of a vector field $X$.

From the definition of $d$, for each fixed time $h\in I$, there exists a horizontal curve $\sigma:[0,\tilde h]\to {\mathbb R}^d$, from ${\bf 0}$ to $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(h)$, parametrized with respect to the (Euclidean) arc length, with 
\begin{equation}\label{Lunghezzadistanza}
\tilde h = {\rm L}_E(\sigma)< 2 d(0, \boldsymbol{\gamma}(h)) \leq 2 h,
\end{equation}
where the last inequality follows from $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ being in arc length.

We point out that, for $h$ small enough,  the curve $\sigma$ will be in $B_E(0,r)$: for all $h\in (0,r/2]$ and $t\in [0,\tilde h]$, we have
$$|\sigma(t) | \leq {\rm L}_E (\sigma) \leq 2d(0, \boldsymbol{\gamma}(h)) \leq 2 h <r.$$
From this last calculation, the estimate (\ref{X2 minore di eps}) holds on $\sigma|_{[0,\tilde{h}]}$.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   

Since $\sigma$ is horizontal, it is absolutely continuous, and $\|\dot\sigma\| = 1$ almost everywhere. Consequently,
$$ |\dot\sigma_d| =\left| \left( \sum_{j=1}^k\langle X_j, \dot\sigma\rangle X_j(\sigma)\right )_d\right| \leq 
   \sum_{j=1}^k\|\dot\sigma\||\left( X_j(\sigma)\right )_d|  =\sum_{j=1}^k |\left( X_j(\sigma)\right )_d|
$$
                                                                                                                                
                                   
Hence, by (\ref{X2 minore di eps}), we deduce
\begin{equation}\label{sigma2}
|\sigma_d(t)|\leq \int_0^t\sum_{j=1}^k|(X_j(\sigma(s)))_d|{\rm d} s\leq k \varepsilon t.
\end{equation}

                                                                                                                              
From (\ref{stima}) and then (\ref{sigma2}), for all $h\in (0,r/2]$ we get
 $$0<c h \stackrel{\eqref{stima}}{<}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_d(h)=\sigma_d(\tilde h)\stackrel{\eqref{sigma2}}{<}k \varepsilon \tilde h.$$
The obtained inequality is in contradiction with \eqref{Lunghezzadistanza} as soon as $\varepsilon$ is taken smaller than $c/(2 k )$. 
We obtained a contradiction that yields the fact that $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is horizontal.

                                                                                                           
Regarding the second part of the statement, for simplicity, we only consider the case when the norm is constantly equal to the Euclidean norm, whereas for the general case, one should localize freezing the norm; see \cite[Proposition 4.2.4]{LeDonneGTM}. We show that for every horizontal curve $\gamma$, we have ${\rm L}_d(\gamma)={\rm L}_E(\gamma).$ Indeed, ${\rm L}_E\leq {\rm L}_d$ since $d_E\leq d,$
and, from the definition of $d$ and the fact that $\gamma$ is horizontal,
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\rm L}_d(\gamma)&\stackrel{\rm def}{=}& \sup_{\mathcal P}\sum_{i}d\left(\gamma(t_i),\gamma(t_{i+1})\right)\\
&\leq& \sup_{\mathcal P}\sum_i {\rm L}_E (\gamma|^{t_{i+1}}_{t_i})\\
&= &\sup_{\mathcal P}{\rm L}_E(\gamma)= {\rm L}_E(\gamma)
\end{eqnarray*}
where the $\sup$ is over the partitions $\mathcal P=\{t_i\}$ of the domain of $\gamma.$ 
\qed

label: eq:EuclCCcompare
title: Proof
body_md:
The statements are local in nature. Fix a point $p\in M$. After restricting to a sufficiently small coordinate neighborhood $U$ of $p$, we may identify $U$ with a bounded open subset of $\mathbb R^d$. We may further assume that $U$ is compactly contained in a larger chart. Since $\Delta$ and $\|\cdot\|$ are continuous, there exists a constant $C\geq 1$ such that \begin{equation}\label{eq:EuclCCcompare} |v|_{\rm Eucl}\leq C\|v\|, \qquad \forall q\in U,\ \forall v\in \Delta_q. \end{equation} Consequently, up to making $U$ smaller we have
\[ d_{\rm Eucl}(x,y)\leq C\, d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y), \qquad \forall x,y\in U. \] 
 
\noindent {\bf (1).} Let $(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n)_{n\in {\mathbb N}}$ be a sequence of curves in $U$ with a common starting point and uniformly bounded CC-length  with \[ L:=\sup_{n\in {\mathbb N}} {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n)<\infty . \] After reparametrizing with bounded speed (e.g. proportionally to arc-length), we may assume \[ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n|_{[s,t]}) \leq L|t-s|, \qquad \forall s,t\in[0,1]. \] By Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability}, \[ {\rm L}_{d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n|_{[s,t]}) = {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n|_{[s,t]}), \] and therefore \[ d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(s),\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)) \leq L|t-s|. \] Using \eqref{eq:EuclCCcompare}, \[ d_{\rm Eucl}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(s),\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)) \leq CL|t-s|. \] Hence the family $(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n)$ is equi-Lipschitz in Euclidean coordinates. Since all curves start at the same point, \[ d_{\rm Eucl}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t),\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(0)) \leq C\, d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t),\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(0)) \leq CL, \] so the images of all $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ lie in a common compact subset of a larger chart. By the Arzelà--Ascoli theorem, a subsequence converges uniformly to a curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}:[0,1]\to M$, with respect to the manifold topology. 
 
\noindent {\bf (2).} In Lemma~\ref{lem:limcurvehorizontal}, we shall prove a more general statement in the setting of varying structures. Thus, \eqref{eq limits of lenths} follows from \eqref{eq limits of lenths - varying}. 

 
\noindent {\bf (3).} Let $x,y$ be sufficiently close to $p$ in the distance $d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|}$. Choose a minimizing sequence of horizontal curves joining $x$ and $y$. By (1), after reparametrization a subsequence converges uniformly to a horizontal curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$. By (2), \[ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) \leq \liminf_n {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n) = d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y). \] Since the opposite inequality follows from the definition of the distance, \[ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) = d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y). \] Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability} now gives \[ {\rm L}_{d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) = d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y). \] Hence every sufficiently small neighborhood is geodesic. 
 
\noindent {\bf (4).} Let $x,y\in M$ and let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose a horizontal curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ joining $x$ to $y$ such that \[ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) \leq d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y)+\varepsilon. \] By Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability}, \[ {\rm L}_{d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) = {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}). \] Therefore \[ d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(x,y) = \inf_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} {\rm L}_{d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}), \] so $d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}$ is an inner metric. 
 
\noindent {\bf (5).} Let $(p_n)$ be a $d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}$-Cauchy sequence contained in a sufficiently small closed neighborhood that is contained in a coordinate neighborhood $U$. From \eqref{eq:EuclCCcompare}, \[ d_{\rm Eucl}(p_n,p_m) \leq C\, d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(p_n,p_m), \] hence $(p_n)$ is Euclidean Cauchy and converges to some $p_\infty\in U$. Passing to a subsequence, we may assume \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(p_n,p_{n+1}) <\infty. \] For each $n$, by (3), choose a geodesic $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ joining $p_n$ to $p_{n+1}$. Concatenating the curves $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ yields a horizontal curve of finite CC-length. By (1) the concatenation converges uniformly to a continuous curve ending at $p_\infty$. Consequently, \[ d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(p_n,p_\infty) \leq \sum_{k=n}^{\infty} d_{\Delta,\|\cdot\|}(p_k,p_{k+1}), \] and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Hence $p_n\to p_\infty$ in the CC metric. Therefore every sufficiently small closed neighborhood is complete.

label: lem:limcurvehorizontal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The assertion is local, so fix a compact subinterval $J\subset I$ and a coordinate neighborhood containing $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(J)$ and, for all sufficiently large $n$, $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(J)$.
We identify this neighborhood with an open subset of $\mathbb R^d$.
All arguments below are on $J$; a decomposition by such intervals gives the result on $I$.

By continuity of the limiting norm and its positive definiteness on $\Delta$, after shrinking the coordinate neighborhood there is $C>0$ such that
\[
 |v|_{\rm eucl}\leq C\|v\|_n , \qquad \forall v\in\Delta_n(q),
\]
for every sufficiently large $n$ and every $q$ in this neighborhood.
 
The uniform CC-speed bound therefore gives a uniform Euclidean $L^\infty$ bound on $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$.
After discarding finitely many indices, the curves are Euclidean Lipschitz with a common constant.
Therefore, also their uniform limit $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is Lipschitz.

Write the locally convergent horizontal frames as
\[
 X^{(n)}_1,\ldots,X^{(n)}_k\longrightarrow X_1,\ldots,X_k
\]
uniformly, where $X_1,\ldots,X_k$ frame $\Delta$.
For almost every $t\in J$, horizontality of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ gives coefficients $a_{nj}(t)$ such that
\[
 \dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_{nj}(t)X^{(n)}_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)).
\]
The frame vectors remain uniformly linearly independent on a possibly smaller neighborhood, so their coefficient maps are uniformly bounded there.
Consequently, the coefficients $a_{nj}$ are uniformly bounded in $L^\infty(J)$.
Passing to a subsequence, for each $j$ we have weak-* convergence in $L^\infty(J)$ of $a_{nj}$ to some $a_j\in L^\infty(J)$, as $n\to \infty$.

The uniform convergence of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ and the frames implies uniform convergence of $X^{(n)}_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(\cdot))$ to $X_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\cdot))$.
Consequently, by the weak-* convergence of $a_{nj}$, we obtain that for all $j$   the sequence 
$a_{nj}(\cdot)X^{(n)}_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(\cdot))$ converges weak-*  to 
$a_{j}(\cdot)X_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\cdot))$.

 Therefore, for each $s,t\in J$, the   weak-* convergence  implies
\begin{align*}
 \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)-\boldsymbol{\gamma}(s)
 &=\lim_{i\to\infty}\int_s^t\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i(u)\,{\rm{d}} u\\
 &=\lim_{i\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^k\int_s^t a_{ij}(u)X^{(i)}_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_i(u))\,{\rm{d}} u\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^k\int_s^t a_j(u)X_j(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(u))\,{\rm{d}} u.
\end{align*}
Consequently, the curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is $\Delta$-horizontal on $I$.

Regarding the lengths, notice that since the sequence of  norms is converging locally uniformly and the sequence of tangent vectors is  weak-* converging, we have  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lscnorms}
\int_J \|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}\| {\rm{d}} t \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_J {\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(\cdot)\|_n} {\rm{d}} t.
\end{equation}
This can be seen in the following way. In local charts, we can identify $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ with vectors in ${\mathbb R}^d$ converging weak-* to $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)$. Now, the norms $\|\cdot\|_n, \|\cdot\|$ also depend on the basepoint of the tangent vector. Thus, we can write them as $\|\cdot\|_{n,t}, \|\cdot\|_t$, where $\|\cdot\|_{n,t}$ is the norm on the tangent space of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)$ and $\|\cdot\|_t$ is the norm at $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)$. The norms vary continuously in $t \in I$, and $\|\cdot\|_{n,t}\to\|\cdot\|_t$ locally uniformly. A standard application of weak-* convergence together with the convexity of the integral expression gives
$$\int_J {\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)\|_t} {\rm{d}} t \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_J {\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)\|}_t {\rm{d}} t.$$
By uniform convergence, and since the curves have uniformly bounded speed, $\lim_{n\to \infty}\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)\|_{n,t}-\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)\|_{t}=0$ and \eqref{eq:lscnorms} follows.

                                                                                                                                                   
Hence, by Fatou's lemma, \[ {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}|_J) = \int_J {\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)\|}\,{\rm{d}} t \leq \liminf_{n\to\infty} \int_J {\|\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(t)\|_n}\,{\rm{d}} t=  \liminf_{n\to\infty} {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|_n}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n|_J). \]

label: lem: approxinv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: approxinv}
Fix $n\in {\mathbb N}$, with $n\geq 2$, and $x_1,\dots, x_{n}\in {\mathbb R}$. 
 Let $m :=\min_{i\neq j}|x_i-x_j|$. The Vandermonde matrix $\mathbf{V}:={\bf Van}(x_1,\dots, x_n)$ is invertible if and only if $m >0$.  
                                                                                                                                                                      
           
             
 Further, if $m >0$, then for all $x_0\in {\mathbb R}$ the matrix
 \[
\mathbf{M} :=\mathbf{D}_{m }^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{x_0}\mathbf{V}
 \]
 is invertible with
    
                                                                     
    
  \[
 \|\mathbf{M}^{-1}\| \leq n^{n-1} \max\{1,M/m \}^{(n-1)^2} ,
 \]
 where $M:=M(x_0):=\max_{i } |x_i-x_0|$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows by direct calculation. We have $$\mathbf{M}={\bf Van}((x_1-x_0)/m ,(x_2-x_0)/m , \dots, (x_n-x_0)/m ),$$ and thus each entry of $\mathbf{M}$ is bounded by $\max\{1,M/m \}^{n-1}$, and thus $\|\mathbf{M}\|\leq n \max\{1,M/m \}^{n-1}$.

    By assumption $|x_i-x_j|\geq m $ for all $i\neq j$ and thus $|\det(\mathbf{M})|\geq 1$. Let $\sigma_i>0$ be the singular values of $\mathbf{M}$ in increasing order. Then $\|\mathbf{M}\|=\sigma_n$ and $\|\mathbf{M}^{-1}\|=\sigma_1^{-1}$. We have 
    \[
    1 \leq |\det(\mathbf{M})|=  \prod_{i=1}^n \sigma_i\leq \|\mathbf{M}\|^{n-1}\sigma_1,
    \]
    and thus
    \[
    \|\mathbf{M}^{-1}\| \leq \|\mathbf{M}\|^{n-1}\leq n^{n-1} \max\{1,M/m \}^{(n-1)^2}.
    \]

body_md:
By the explicit flows in \eqref{flows}, we have 
$$ (\mathbf{p}^{k+1})_i  = y_k f(p_1+t_k)^{i-2} + (\mathbf{p}^{k})_i, \qquad \forall i\in \{2,\ldots, d\}, \forall k\in\{1, \ldots, d-1\} $$
and
$$ (\mathbf{p}^{k+1})_1  =  (\mathbf{p}^{k})_1, \qquad \forall k\in\{1, \ldots, d-1\} .$$
Thus, by induction, one shows for each $k\in\{1,\dots, d\}$ that
\[
(\mathbf{p}^k)_1=p_1\quad \text{ and } \quad (\mathbf{p}^k)_i = (\mathbf{p})_i + \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} f(p_1+t_j)^{i-2} y_j,\qquad \forall i\in \{2,\ldots, d\} .
\]
Thus, $\mathbf{p}^{d}=\mathbf{p} + (0,{\bf Van}(f(p_1+t_1), \dots, f(p_1+t_{d-1}) )\mathbf{y})$. Applying the final flow $e^{t_{d}\mathbf{X}}$ to $\mathbf{p}^{d}$ yields   \eqref{Madrid19052026_15}.

For the second part of the claim, the first part of the proof and the definitions of $\mathbf{V}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ give
                                                                                               
$$\mathbf{p}^{d+1}=\mathbf{p} + (t_{d},{\bf Van}(f(p_1+t_1), \dots f(p_1+t_{d-1}))\mathbf{y} )=\mathbf{q}.$$
The points give a horizontal curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ of length \eqref{eq:gamlen} connecting $\mathbf{p}$ to $\mathbf{q}$:
\begin{eqnarray*} 
\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})&\leq& 
{\rm L}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})\\
&\stackrel{\eqref{eq:gamlen}}{=}& |t_d|+\sum_{i=1}^{d-1} \left(2|t_i| + |y_i|\right)\\
&= & |p_1-q_1| + \sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\left(2|t_i| +  |(\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1}))_i| \right)\\
&\leq&
|p_1-q_1| + 2d (\max_{i\in \{1,\dots,d-1\}}|t_i| )+d |\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})|.
\end{eqnarray*}

title: Proof
body_md:
If $f$ is constant, then $\mathbf{Y}=(0,1,f(p_1), \dots, f(p_1)^{d-2})$ and $\mathbf{X}=(1,0,\dots, 0)$ are constant vector fields and clearly the claim follows, because only points that differ by $ t \mathbf{X} + s\mathbf{Y}$, for some   $ t,s\in {\mathbb R}$ can be connected. Next, if $I\subset {\mathbb R}$ is an interval such that $f|_{2I}$ is constant and $p_1,q_1\in I$, then unless $\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1}=(s,f(p_1)s, \dots, f(p_1)^{d-2}s)$, every horizontal curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ connecting them must have a first coordinate $\gamma_1$ that leaves the interval $2I$ and re-enters. This yields the desired lower bound for the length by a simple argument as in \eqref{eq:p1bound}. 

Next, for the claimed equation \eqref{eq bounds for d}, we first prove the lower bound for the distance, and hence for the length of any curve joining the points.
Assume that $\boldsymbol{\gamma}=(\gamma_1,\dots, \gamma_d)=(\gamma_1,\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{-1}):[0,1]\to {\mathbb R}^d$ is a horizontal curve between $\mathbf{q} $ and $\mathbf{p} $.
                                                                                                        
Note that $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{-1}'(t)=\gamma_2'(t)\mathbf{Y}_{-1}({\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)})$. 
If the first coordinate $\gamma_1$ of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ takes  some values outside the interval $2I$, then the length of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ would exceed $|I|$, and we get the lower bound by a simple argument as in \eqref{eq:p1bound}. 
                                                                                                                     
Suppose instead that  $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is such that $\gamma_1$ takes values within $2I$. 
We are going to give a different lower bound for $\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})$. 
To do so, we are going to use the matrices
$\mathbf{D}_{\delta} $ and $\mathbf{L}_a$ defined in \eqref{eq:def:D} and \eqref{eq:def:L}, respectively, and we see them as acting on ${\mathbb R}^{n}$, with $n:=d-1$, seen inside ${\mathbb R}^d$ as those points that have 0 first coordinate. In particular, 
since the first component of $\mathbf{Y}=(0,\mathbf{Y}_{-1})\simeq \mathbf{Y}$ vanishes, we identify it with a vector in ${\mathbb R}^{d-1}$.
                          
Then, using the definitions, together with \eqref{eq L applied}, we calculate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:calcolo}
\mathbf{D}_{\delta^{-1}}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}\mathbf{Y}_{-1}({\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)}) = \sum_{i=2}^{d} \left(\frac{f(\gamma_1(t))-f(p_1)}{\delta}\right)^{i-2}\partial_i.
\end{equation}
Noticing that each coordinate of this last vector field has absolute value at most one, we bound:
\begin{eqnarray*}
 \left|\mathbf{D}_{\delta^{-1}}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})\right | 
&=&
\left |\mathbf{D}_{\delta^{-1}}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{-1}(1)-\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{-1}(0))\right|
\\
&=&
\left|
\int_0^1 \dfrac{{\rm{d}}}{{\rm{d}} t}
\mathbf{D}_{\delta^{-1}}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{-1}(t){\rm{d}} t\right| \\
&=&
\left|
\int_0^1 
\mathbf{D}_{\delta^{-1}}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}\gamma_{2}'(t)\mathbf{Y}_{-1}({\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)}){\rm{d}} t\right| \\
&\stackrel{\eqref{eq:calcolo}}{\leq} &
d \int_0^1 
|\gamma_{2}'(t)|
 {\rm{d}} t \leq d\,{\rm L}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}).
\end{eqnarray*}
In addition, we have another bound: 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:p1bound}
|p_1-q_1|=\left| \int_0^1 \gamma_1'(t){\rm{d}} t \right| \leq \int_0^1 |\gamma_1'(t)|{\rm{d}} t \leq {\rm L}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}).
\end{equation}
Taking the average of the previous two lower bounds for ${\rm L}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})$ and taking the infimum over $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$, we get the lower bound in \eqref{eq bounds for d}. 



Regarding the upper bound in \eqref{eq bounds for d}, the assumption on the $s_i$'s implies that the Vandermonde matrix $\mathbf{V}$ is invertible. Take 
$t_i:=s_i-p_1$, for $i\in \{1,\ldots, d-1\}$,
$t_d:=q_1-p_1$, and $\mathbf{y} := \mathbf{V}
                                     
^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})$. 
Lemma~\ref{lem: simpleflow} gives a chain of points from $\mathbf{p}$ to $\mathbf{q}$.
In addition, notice that $$
|p_1-q_1| \leq |I|\quad \text{ and } \quad
|t_i| = |s_i-p_1| \leq 2|I|,$$
since $s_i\in 2I$ and $p_1\in I$.
The upper bound in \eqref{eq bounds for d} then follows from the estimate \eqref{Madrid19052026_16}.
                   

Finally, if $s_1,\dots, s_{d-1}$ is chosen so that 
                                
$f(s_{1}) ,\dots, f(s_{d-1})$ 
is an equi-partition of $f(2I)$, then $m:=\min_{i\neq j} |f(s_{i})-f(s_{j})|=\frac{\delta}{d-2} $  
and $M:=\max_{i }|f(s_{i})-f(p_{1})|\leq \delta$. 
So, for the matrix 
$\mathbf{M} :=\mathbf{D}_{m }^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}\mathbf{V}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem: approxinv}, applied with $x_0:=f(p_1)$ and $x_i:=f(s_i)$, gives 
\begin{equation}\label{eq-bound-M}
     \|\mathbf{M}^{-1}\| \leq n^{n-1} \max\{1,M/m \}^{(n-1)^2} 
\leq (d-1)^{d-2} (d-2 )^{(d-2)^2} ,
\end{equation}
which only depends on $d$. Moreover, we bound one of the terms in the right-hand side of \eqref{eq bounds for d} as
\begin{eqnarray*}
    d\left|\mathbf{V}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})\right|
    &=& d\left| \mathbf{M}^{-1}   \mathbf{D}_{m }^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})\right|\\
&\leq&  
    d\,\| \mathbf{M}^{-1} \|\,\| \mathbf{D}_{d-2} \|\,\left| \mathbf{D}_{\delta}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})\right|,
\end{eqnarray*}
where we have used that $\mathbf{D}_{m } = \mathbf{D}_{\delta/(d-2) }= \mathbf{D}_{\delta} \mathbf{D}_{d-2}^{-1} $.
Consequently, together with the bound \eqref{eq-bound-M}, we get the final estimate \eqref{eq another bounds for d} for a suitable $C_d$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By construction, the function $\mathbf{d}$ is constructed via a length structure (in the sense of \cite[Section~2.1.1]{bbi}), is symmetric, and satisfies the triangle inequality. Moreover, for every compact set $K\subseteq {\mathbb R}^d$, the function $f$ is bounded on the first-coordinate projection of $K$, being continuous. Thus, the Euclidean norms of the vector fields $\mathbf{X}_f$ and $\mathbf{Y}_f$ can a bounded on $K$. Therefore, for any compact set, there exists $C>0$ such that $\mathbf{d}_{\rm eucl}\leq C \mathbf{d}$ holds on this set. In particular, the function $\mathbf{d}$ is positive.

If $f$ is constant, then Clause (1) in Lemma~\ref{lem: distest} says that $\mathbf{d}$ is not finite-valued. If $f$ is not constant, for all $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ there is a large enough interval $I$ such that \eqref{eq another bounds for d} gives a finite value.

If $f$ does not have positive oscillation, then it is constant in some interval. Thus,  by Clause (2) in Lemma~\ref{lem: distest}, we get a different topology.
Suppose next that  $f$ has positive oscillation. On the one hand,  the local property $\mathbf{d}_{\rm eucl}\leq C \mathbf{d}$ tells us that $\mathbf{p} \to \mathbf{q} $ in the Euclidean topology if $  \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\to 0$. On the other hand, 
if $\mathbf{p} \to \mathbf{q} $, then \eqref{eq another bounds for d} gives $  \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\to 0$, by choosing $I$ small enough (fixing $\delta>0$).

label: thm: ballbox
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: ballbox}
Given $d\in {\mathbb N}$ with $d\geq 3$ there exists $c_d\in(0,1)$ with the following property: Let $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ be continuous and let   $\mathbf{d}:=\mathbf{d}_f$ be as in \eqref{eq:metricdef} via the vector fields \eqref{eq:vectdef}.
Assume that $\operatorname{osc}(f,I)>0$ for every interval $I\subset {\mathbb R}$.
                                         
 Then, for every $\mathbf{p}                  
 \in {\mathbb R}^d$ and every $ r>0$ we have
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}( {\mathbf{Box}}(\delta_1,c_d r))
                                                                                                                   
 \subset B_\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},r) \subset 
\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}( {\mathbf{Box}}(\delta_2, 2dr)),
                                                                                     
\end{eqnarray*}
 
                  
                                                                                                                                          
                                                                                             
                
where $\delta_1:=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-{2 c_d r} ,p_1+{2 c_d r}])$ and $\delta_2:=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-2r,p_1+2r])$.
head: environment
name: Ball-Box Theorem

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $\mathbf{p} =(p_1,\mathbf{p}_{-1})\in {\mathbb R}^d$ and $r>0$.
Let $I:= [p_1-cr,p_1+cr]$ with $c=c_d\in(0,1)$ to be chosen; so $\delta_1=\operatorname{osc}(f,2 I)$.
Let $\mathbf{q}=(q_1,\mathbf{q}_{-1})\in \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}( {\mathbf{Box}}(\delta_1,c r))$. Therefore, we have $|p_1-q_1|\leq cr$ and 
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})
\in [-cr,cr]  \times \left[ -cr\delta_1 , cr\delta_1 \right]\times   \left[-cr\delta_1^{2},cr\delta_1^{2}\right]\times\cdots \times  \left [-cr\delta_1^{d-2},cr\delta_1^{d-2}\right].
\end{equation*}
From this, we get
\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{D}_{\delta_1}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})
\in [-cr,cr]  ^{d-1}.
\end{equation*}
Thus, $|\mathbf{D}_{\delta_1}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})|\leq cr \sqrt{d-1}$.
Apply \eqref{eq another bounds for d} in Lemma~\ref{lem: distest} with $I $ defined above 
                      
to obtain, for some  constant $C_d\geq 1$,  
\[
\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\leq C_d\left (2cr+|\mathbf{D}_{\delta_1}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})|\right) \leq C_dc\left(2+\sqrt{d-1}\right) r.
\] 
Once $c$ is chosen smaller than $ \frac{1}{C_d(2+\sqrt{d-1})}$, the first containment in the statement follows. 

For the second containment, take any $\mathbf{q}\in B_{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{p},r)$, so $|p_1-q_1|\leq\mathbf{d} (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})< r$. We apply \eqref{eq bounds for d} from Lemma~\ref{lem: distest} with $I:=[p_1-r,p_1+r]$, having $p_1,q_1\in I$. We get 
\[
\frac{1}{2}|p_1-q_1|+\frac{1}{2d}|\mathbf{D}_{\delta_2}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})|\leq r,
\]
and thus  
\[
\left|\mathbf{D}_{\delta_2}^{-1}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})\right|\leq 2dr.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{q}_{-1}&\in \mathbf{p}_{-1}+\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{D}_{\delta_2}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}[-2dr,2dr]\right)\right).
\end{align*}
Since we also had $|p_1-q_1|< r< 2dr$ , we conclude that $\mathbf{q}\in \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}( {\mathbf{Box}}(\delta_2, 2dr))$.

label: eq:volbounds
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f:{\mathbb R}\to{\mathbb R}$ be a continuous function that has doubling oscillation. Recall that $\det(\mathbf{L}_{a})=1$. Therefore, $\mathbf{T}_\mathbf{p}$ is volume preserving for every $\mathbf{p}\in {\mathbb R}^d$, and we get from Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox}
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:volbounds}
        \delta_1(r)^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}} (2c_d r)^d\leq \lambda(B(\mathbf{p},r)) \leq \delta_2(r)^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}} (4dr)^d
    \end{equation}
    for $\delta_1(r):=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-2c_dr, p_1+2c_d r])$ and $\delta_2(r):=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-2r, p_1+2r])$. Since $f$ has doubling oscillation, for some constant $c>1$ we have $\delta_2(2r)\leq c\delta_1(r)$. Thus
    \[
    \lambda(B(\mathbf{p},2r))\leq \delta_2(2r)^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}} (8dr)^d \leq c^{\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}} \left(\frac{4d}{c_d}\right)^d\lambda(B(\mathbf{p},r)).
    \]
    This gives the doubling property. Similarly, by doubling, since $\delta_1(r)$  and $\delta_2(r)$ are both comparable to $\rho=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r])$, we get \eqref{eq measure expansion}.

    For the Ahlfors regularity, the argument is similar. First, $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_f)$ is unbounded since it is boundedly compact and homeomorphic to ${\mathbb R}^d$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}. Note that $\alpha$-regular oscillation implies that 
    \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r]) &\leq C \operatorname{osc}(f,[-r-|p_1|-1,r+|p_1|+1])\left(\frac{r}{r+1+|p_1|}\right)^\alpha \\
    &\leq C^2 \operatorname{osc}(f,[-1,+1])r^\alpha,
    \end{align*}
    and
    \begin{align*}
    \operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r]) &\geq C^{-1} \operatorname{osc}(f,[-r-|p_1|-1,r+|p_1|+1])\left(\frac{r}{r+1+|p_1|}\right)^\alpha \\
    &\geq C^{-2} \operatorname{osc}(f,[-1,+1])r^\alpha.
    \end{align*}
    This, together with \eqref{eq:volbounds} gives Ahlfors-regularity with $Q=d+\frac{(d-2)(d-1)}{2}\alpha$ since here $\rho$ is comparable to $r^\alpha$.

    Finally, each set $\mathbf{Box}(\delta,r)$ is convex in ${\mathbb R}^d$ and can be contracted to the point $\mathbf{0}$ by homotheties, and this contraction has an image contained in $\mathbf{Box}(\delta,r)$. Therefore, by Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox} we can contract $B_{\mathbf{d}_f}(\mathbf{p},r)$ to $\{\mathbf{p}\}$ within the set $\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{Box}(\delta_2(r),2dr))$. Let $R=\frac{2dr}{c_d}$. Then 
    \[
    \mathbf{Box}(\delta_2(r),2dr) \subset \mathbf{Box}(\delta_1(R), c_dR),
    \]
    and by Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox} 
    \[
    \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{Box}(\delta_2(r),2dr)) \subset \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}(\mathbf{Box}(\delta_1(R), c_dR)) \subset B_{\mathbf{d}_f}(\mathbf{p}, R)
    \]
    and LLC follows.

title: Remark
body_md: There are many constructions of $\alpha$-regular functions, and we present only one. An interesting construction is obtained by constructing functions whose graphs are Bedford-McMullen carpets. This procedure is used in \cite[Example 4.8]{Cdim} to construct a function $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$, and one can see that their construction produces a function that has $\alpha$-regular oscillation (with the natural modification of the definition for a map defined only on $[0,1]$). We refer to this reference for details of the construction and sketch briefly how regularity follows. One obtains the graph of such $f$ as an attractor of a self-affine iterated function system where the $x$-direction is scaled by $1/m$ and the $y$-direction by $1/\ell$ for some integers $m>\ell\geq 2$. It follows from this, as \cite[Figure 4.2]{Cdim} shows well, that the image of every $m$-adic interval $I$ of length $m^{-k}$ in $[0,1]$ under $f$ is an $\ell$-adic interval of length $\ell^{-k}$. Let $\alpha=\log_{m}(\ell)\in (0,1)$. The lower bound for $\alpha$-regular oscillation is obtained by the fact that every interval in $[0,1]$ contains an $m$-adic interval of comparable length. The upper bound is obtained similarly since every interval is contained in at most two adjacent $m$-adic intervals of comparable length. While this procedure constructs a function on $[0,1]$, a function $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ can be obtained from this by taking a subsequential limit of maps $g_r(x)=(f(x_0+rx)-f(x_0))r^{-\alpha}$ as $r\searrow 0$ and $x_0\in(0,1)$ and applying the Arzel\'a-Ascoli theorem.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove an oscillation upper bound for $b$-adic intervals. Fix $m\in {\mathbb Z}$ and consider any interval $I_{k,m}:=[kb^{-m}, (k+1)b^{-m}]$ of length $b^{-m}$ for $k\in {\mathbb Z}$. Fix $N\in {\mathbb N}$, whose precise value will be determined later. We divide the sum for $f$ as in \eqref{Weierstrass} according to frequencies into the low, mid, and high frequency   terms 
\[
f^{m,-}(x):=\sum_{n\leq m-N} a^n \sin(2\pi b^n x), \ \ \ \ f^{m,+}(x):=\sum_{n\geq m+N} a^n \sin(2\pi b^n x)
\]
\[
f^{m,\sim}(x):=\sum_{m-N < n< m+N} a^n \sin(2\pi b^n x).
\]

By estimating the sum for $f^{m,+}$ from above by a geometric sum, we obtain
\[
\operatorname{osc}\left(f^{m,+}, I_{k,m}\right)\leq 2\|f^{m,+}\|_{L^\infty} \leq 2 \frac{a^{m+N}}{1-a}.
\]
By using the mean value theorem on each term of $f^{m,-}$, we get
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{osc}\left(f^{m,-}, I_{k,m}\right)&\leq \sum_{n\leq m-N} \operatorname{osc}(a^n \sin(2\pi b^n x), I_{k,m}) \\
&\leq \sum_{n\leq m-N} 2\pi \left(ab\right)^n b^{-m} \\
&\leq 2\pi\frac{(ab)^{m-N+1}}{ab-1} b^{-m}=2\pi \frac{a^{m-N+1}}{ab-1} b^{1-N}.
\end{align*}
Choose $N\geq 3$ so big that 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq small oscillation tales}
\operatorname{osc}(f^{m,-}, I_{k,m})\leq a^{m}/8\quad \text{  and } \quad \operatorname{osc}(f^{m,+}, I_{k,m})\leq a^m / 8,\qquad \forall k,m. 
\end{equation}

Regarding $f^{m,\sim}$, counting the $2N-1$ terms and using $\operatorname{osc}(a^n\sin)\leq2a^n$ 
gives $\operatorname{osc}(f^{m,\sim}, I_{k,m}) \leq 2(2N-1)a^{m-N}$.

Consequently,  
\begin{eqnarray*}
\operatorname{osc}\left(f, I_{k,m}\right) &\leq& \operatorname{osc}\left(f^{m,\sim}, I_{k,m}\right) + \operatorname{osc}\left(f^{m,+}, I_{k,m}\right) + \operatorname{osc}\left(f^{m,-}, I_{k,m}\right) \\
&\leq&
2(2N-1)a^{m-N}+a^{m}/8+a^{m}/8\\
&\leq& 4 N a^{m-N}.
\end{eqnarray*}
For each $I\subset {\mathbb R}$ with $|I|>0$ we can choose some $m\in {\mathbb Z}$ so that $|I|\in [b^{-m}, b^{1-m})$. The interval $I$ intersects at most $2b$ intervals $I_{k,m}$, for $k\in {\mathbb Z}$, and thus we get
\[
\operatorname{osc}(f,I)\leq 2b(4N)a^{m-N}\leq 8bNa^{-N} |I|^\alpha ,
\]
since $|I|^\alpha \in [a^{m}, a^{m-1})$. This yields the upper bound \eqref{eq:defregosc0} for the $\alpha$-regularity. 

The lower bound for the $\alpha$-regularity is trickier and requires Fourier analysis. 
Consider an arbitrary interval $I\subset {\mathbb R}$ with midpoint $x$.
For the $N$ chosen above for \eqref{eq small oscillation tales}, pick $m\in {\mathbb Z}$ so that $6b^{-m+N} \leq |I| < 6b^{-m+N+1}$.   Choose $k\in {\mathbb Z}$ so that $x\in I_{k,m}$.
Given these $k,m\in {\mathbb Z}$, there exists a unique $l=l(k,m)$ with $I_{k,m}\subset I_{l ,m-N}$. By orthogonality,
\[
\int_{I_{l,m-N}} \left(f^{m,\sim}(t)-f^{m,\sim}(t+b^{-m}/2)\right)\sin(2 \pi b^m t){\rm{d}} t = a^m b^{N-m}.
\]
Thus, there exists some $t\in I_{l,m-N}$ for which $|f^{m,\sim}(t)-f^{m,\sim}(t+b^{-m}/2)|\geq a^m$. The points $t$ and $t+b^{-m}/2$ lie in 
the same or adjacent $b$-adic intervals of length $b^{-m}$.
Therefore, for at least one of these intervals, say $I_{z,m}$, for some $z$, the oscillation is at least half of $a^m$, i.e.,  
\[
\operatorname{osc}(f^{m,\sim}, I_{z,m})\geq a^m/2.
\]
But, for this interval, we get
\[
\operatorname{osc}(f,I_{z,m}) \geq \operatorname{osc}(f^{m,\sim}, I_{z,m})-\operatorname{osc}(f^{m,-}, I_{z,m})-\operatorname{osc}(f^{m,+}, I_{z,m})\geq a^m/4.
\]
The interval $I_{z,m}$ is contained in either $I_{l,m-N}$ or one of its neighbors. In either case, because of the length of $I$, we have
$I_{z,m}\subset   I$.
                                                  
                                                                                                              
In particular, 
\[
\operatorname{osc}(f,I)\geq \operatorname{osc}(f,I_{z,m})\geq a^m/4 = \frac{\left(b^{-m}\right)^{\alpha}}{4}\geq 4^{-1}\left(\frac{|I|}{6 b^{N+1}}\right)^\alpha.
\]
Thus,
\[
\operatorname{osc}(f, I)\geq C_{\alpha}|I|^\alpha,
\]
where $C_{\alpha}:=4^{-1}6^{-\alpha}b^{-(N+1)\alpha}$. This gives the lower bound \eqref{eq:defregosc0} for the oscillation of $f$ and thus the $\alpha$-regularity.

title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lem:equicont} Let $D>1, (\epsilon,\delta)\in (0,1)^2$. If $\mathcal{F} \subset \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon, \delta}$ is a collection of functions with $f(0)=0$ and $ \operatorname{osc}(f,[-1,1])=1$, for every $f\in \mathcal{F}$, then $\mathcal{F}$ is pre-compact in the topology of locally uniform convergence.

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem, it suffices to show that the family $\mathcal{F}$ is locally uniformly equicontinuous and equibounded. Fix $R\geq 1$. By repeatedly using that  oscillation is doubling, we have $\operatorname{osc}(f,[-4R,4R]) \leq M:=\operatorname{osc}(f,[-1,1])\cdot D^{\log_2(R)+3}$ for all $f\in \mathcal{F}.$ This implies local equiboundedness since $f(0)=0$ for all $f\in \mathcal{F}$.

    For the equicontinuity fix $\overline{\epsilon}>0$.  First, choose a $k_0\in {\mathbb N}$, such that  $M\epsilon^{k_0}\leq \overline{\epsilon}$. Let $\overline{\delta}=R\delta^{k_0}$. Now, let $x,y\in [-R,R]$ with $|x-y|\leq \overline{\delta}$ and $n\in {\mathbb N}$ be arbitrary. For the segment $J=[x,y]$ we have by the reverse doubling property:
    \[
    \operatorname{osc}(f,J)\leq \epsilon^{k_0} \operatorname{osc}(f, \delta^{-k_0} J) \leq \epsilon^{k_0} \operatorname{osc}(f,[-4R,4R])\leq \overline{\epsilon}.
    \]
    Here, we used the fact that $\delta^{-k_0} J$ has length at most $R$, and thus is contained in the interval $[-4R,4R]$. Since $\overline{\epsilon},R$ were arbitrary, equicontinuity follows.

label: lem: convergence
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: convergence} Let $D>1, \epsilon,\delta\in (0,1)$.  Let $(c_n)_{n\in {\mathbb N}}$ be a sequence of positive scalars with $c_n\to c>0$.
 Assume that $(f_n)_{n\in {\mathbb N}}$ is a sequence of continuous functions with $f_n \in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon, \delta}$ for every $n\in {\mathbb N}$, that converges locally uniformly to a non-constant function $f$. Then $f\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon, \delta}$ and the sequence
 \[
 ({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f_n},c_n\lambda, \mathbf{0})
 \]
 pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff converges to 
 \[
 ({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f},c\lambda,\mathbf{0}).
 \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will argue that we can choose the Hausdorff approximating sequence $\phi_n={\rm id}$, and this will give the pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. For this sequence of maps, the vague convergence of measures is trivial, and all we need to prove is the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff convergence with this particular choice of approximating sequence. This can be reduced with \cite[Proposition 12.1.3]{LeDonneGTM} to local uniform convergence of the distance functions $\mathbf{d}_{f_n} \to \mathbf{d}_{f} $. Next, we verify two uniform estimates that are needed to apply this proposition.


First, the sequence $(f_n)_{n\in {\mathbb N}}$ converges locally uniformly to $f$ and thus $f$ is continuous. Local uniform convergence implies that for every interval $J\subset {\mathbb R}$ we have $\lim_{n\to \infty} \operatorname{osc}(f_n,J)=\operatorname{osc}(f,J)$. Since the doubling and reverse doubling inequalities are stable under limits, this implies $f\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon, \delta}$. Since $f$ is not constant, there is some interval $I$ such that  $\operatorname{osc}(f, I)>0$. By applying doubling repeatedly, we get that $\operatorname{osc}(f, J)>0$ for every interval $J\subset {\mathbb R}$ and $f$ has positive oscillation. Thus, $\mathbf{d}_f$ induces the Euclidean topology on ${\mathbb R}^d$ by Lemma~\ref{lem: characterization}.

Next, we argue that the family of metrics $\mathbf{d}_{f_n}$ is locally equicontinuous in the following sense. For every $R>0$ and $\epsilon>0$ there exists a $\delta>0$ such that  $|\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{q}|\leq \delta$ and $|\mathbf{p}|, |\mathbf{q}|\leq R$ imply $\mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})\leq \epsilon$ for all $n\in {\mathbb N}$. Fix $\epsilon>0, R>0$. By local uniform convergence, there is an upper bound $M\geq 1$ such that  $\sup_{|x|\leq 2R}|f_n(x)| \leq M$ for all $n\in {\mathbb N}$. Similarly, there is a lower bound $\omega>0$ such that  $\operatorname{osc}(f_n,[-2R,2R]) \geq \omega$ for all $n\in {\mathbb N}$. Let $c_d\in (0,1)$ be the constant from Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox}. By iterating the doubling bound, we get an $\eta\in (0,1)$ such that  for all $p_1\in [-R,R]$ we have $\operatorname{osc}(f_n,[p_1-2c_d\epsilon,p_1+2c_d\epsilon]) \geq \eta$ for all $n\in {\mathbb N}$.


 By the Ball-Box Theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox}, we have 
\[
\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}^{f_n}(\mathbf{Box}(\eta,c_d\epsilon))\subset B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(\mathbf{p},\epsilon).
\]
The matrix $\mathbf{L}_{f_n(p_1)}$ has entries bounded in absolute value by $(dM)^d$, and thus its operator norm is bounded by $d(dM)^{d}$. Thus, if $\delta=\frac{1}{2d(dM)^{d}}\min(\eta,c_d\epsilon\eta^{d-2})$ and $|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}|\leq \delta$, then 
\[
\left(\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}^{f_n}\right)^{-1}(\mathbf{q})=(q_1-p_1,\mathbf{L}_{f_n(p_1)}(\mathbf{q}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1}))\in \mathbf{Box}(\eta,c_d\epsilon)
\]
and $\mathbf{q} \in \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{p}}^{f_n}(\mathbf{Box}(\eta,c_d\epsilon))$. Therefore, $\mathbf{q} \in B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(\mathbf{p},\epsilon)$ and we get $\mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{p})\leq \epsilon$. This yields the desired equicontinuity.

Next, we establish a uniform boundedness principle. Let $R>0$. As before, there exists an $M\geq 1$ such that  $\operatorname{osc}(f_n,[-2R,2R]) \leq M$ and $|f_n(0)|\leq M$ for all $n\in {\mathbb N}$.  By the Ball-Box Theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox},  we have
\[
B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(0,R)\subset \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{0}}^{f_n}(\mathbf{Box}(M,2dR)).
\]
Since the operator norm of $\mathbf{L}^{-1}_{f_n(0)}$ is bounded by $d(dM)^{d}$, we have 
\[
\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{0}}^{f_n}(\mathbf{Box}(M,2dR)) \subset [-2dR,2dR] \times \mathbf{L}^{-1}_{f_n(0)}(B(0,2d^{3/2}R M^{d-2})) \subset B(0,4 M^{2d-2} d^{d+5/2} R).
\]
This yields $\bigcup_{n\in {\mathbb N}} B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(0,R)\subset B(0,4 M^{2d-2} d^{d+5/2} R)$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}, we have 
\[
\operatorname{diam}_{\mathbf{d}_f}\left(\bigcup_{n\in {\mathbb N}} B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(0,R)\right)<\infty \ \ \forall R>0.
\]
This verifies the main assumption of \cite[Proposition 12.1.3]{LeDonneGTM}, and what remains is to prove that $\mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})\to \mathbf{d}_f(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})$ uniformly when $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}$ lie in an arbitrary bounded subset. By local uniform equicontinuity of the metrics, it suffices to prove this pointwise. Thus, fix $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\in {\mathbb R}^d$.


Denote by $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}_{f_n}, \mathbf{Y}_f$ the vector fields as defined in \eqref{eq:vectdef}, with the added subscript indicating the function used. Let $\Delta_n$ ($\Delta$) be the horizontal bundle spanned by $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}_{f_n}$ ($\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}_f$), and let $\|\cdot\|_n$ ($\|\cdot\|$) be a continuous norm on the tangent space of ${\mathbb R}^d$ whose restriction to $\Delta_n$ ($\Delta$) corresponds to the inner product norm induced by declaring $\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}_{f_n}$ ($\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}_{f}$) orthonormal. We may assume $\|\cdot\|_n\to \|\cdot\|$.

Our objective is to show for all $\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}\in {\mathbb R}^d$ that
 \begin{equation}\label{lim dist}
      \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})=\mathbf{d}_f(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}).
  \end{equation}
We will reduce this to two inequalities. First, pass to a subsequence realizing the limit inferior $\liminf_{n\to \infty} \mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})$. Then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}, we may choose geodesics $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ connecting $\mathbf{p}$ to $\mathbf{q}$ for $\mathbf{d}_{f_n}$ such that  ${\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|_n}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n)=\mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})$. Since the metrics are uniformly bounded, these curves have uniformly bounded length and can be parameterized by uniformly bounded speed. These curves have also uniformly bounded Euclidean length, since $f_n$ are uniformly bounded on bounded sets, and thus we may extract a subsequence that converges uniformly in ${\mathbb R}^d$ to a curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:limcurvehorizontal}, we have
\[
\mathbf{d}_{f}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}) \leq {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}) \leq \liminf_{n\to \infty}{\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|_n}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n)=\liminf_{n\to \infty} \mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}).
\]
This gives one of the inequalities for \eqref{lim dist}, and we just need an opposite one for the limit superior.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}, there exists a geodesic $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ with $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(0)=\mathbf{p}$ to $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(1)=\mathbf{q}$ for $\mathbf{d}_{f}$ such that  ${\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})=\mathbf{d}_{f}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})$. By Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability}, the curve $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ is horizontal and thus for a.e. $t$ in its domain $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma} = a(t) \mathbf{X}+b(t)\mathbf{Y}_{f}$. By Remark~\ref{rmk endpoint}, we can find $\Delta_n$-horizontal curves $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n$ with $\dot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n = a(t) \mathbf{X}+b(t)\mathbf{Y}_{f_n}$ that start at $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(0)=\mathbf{p}$ and $\lim_{n\to \infty} |\boldsymbol{\gamma}(1)-\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(1)|=0$. By equicontinuity of the metrics, we also get
\[
\lim_{n\to \infty} \sup_{m\in {\mathbb N}} \mathbf{d}_{f_m}(\mathbf{q},\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(1))=0.
\]
Thus,
\begin{align*}
\limsup_{n\to \infty} \mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})&\leq \limsup_{n\to \infty} \left(\mathbf{d}_{f_n}(\mathbf{p},\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(1))+\sup_{m\in {\mathbb N}} \mathbf{d}_{f_m}(\mathbf{q},\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n(1))\right) \\
&\leq \limsup_{n\to \infty} {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|_n}(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_n) \\
&=\limsup_{n\to \infty} {\rm L}_{\|\cdot\|}(\boldsymbol{\gamma})  = \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}).
\end{align*}

label: lem: rescaling
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: rescaling} Let $D>1, r>0, \mathbf{p}\in {\mathbb R}^d$ and $\epsilon,\delta \in (0,1)$. If $f\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$, then for all $c>0$ the pointed metric measure space
\[
({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f}/r,c\lambda,\mathbf{p})
\]
is isomorphic to
\[
({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{g},c'\lambda,0)
\] 
for some $c'>0$, and some $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ with $g(0)=0$ and $\operatorname{osc}(g,[-1,1])=1$. In fact, one can choose $g(x):=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r])^{-1}(f(p_1+rx)-f(p_1))$. If, moreover, $f\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$, then this choice gives $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\rho:=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r])^{-1}$ and $g$ be as in the statement.  Define 
 \[
F((x_1,\mathbf{x}_{-1})):=((x_1-p_1)/r,\mathbf{D}_{\rho}\mathbf{L}_{f(p_1)}(\mathbf{x}_{-1}-\mathbf{p}_{-1})/r).
 \] 
 Then a direct calculation gives $DF(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{X}_{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{X}(F(\mathbf{x}))/r$ and $DF(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{Y}_{f}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{Y}_{g}(F(\mathbf{x}))/r$. Thus, $F$ maps horizontal curves with respect to $\Delta_f$ to a horizontal curve with respect to $\Delta_g$, and $F^{-1}$ vice versa. The map $DF$ scales horizontal vectors by factor $1/r$, and thus is an isometry between $\mathbf{d}_f/r$ and $\mathbf{d}_g$. Next, $DF$ has constant Jacobian, and thus the claim follows by choosing $c'=c/|\det(DF)|$.

 The classes $\mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ and $\mathcal{F}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$ are invariant under scaling and thus the claims on $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ and $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$ follow.

title: Theorem
body_md:

${\mathcal M}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$ and ${\mathcal M}^{\rm doubl}_{D, \epsilon, \delta}$ are invariant under scalings and changes of basepoints, and compact with respect to pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence.

title: Proof
body_md:
We focus on ${\mathcal M}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ since the case of regular functions is identical. 

 Next, we argue invariance under scalings and translations. Let $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f},c\lambda, \mathbf{p})\in {\mathcal M}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$  and $\mathbf{q}\in {\mathbb R}^d$ and $r>0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem: rescaling}, we have  that the space $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f}/r,\lambda/ \lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_f}(\mathbf{q},r)), \mathbf{q})$ is isomorphic to $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{g},d'\lambda, \mathbf{0})$ for some $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$. The isomorphism preserves the volume of the unit ball, and thus $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f}/r,\lambda/ \lambda(B(\mathbf{q},r)), \mathbf{q}) \sim ({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{g},d'\lambda, \mathbf{0}) \in {\mathcal M}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$. 
 
 Next, we argue convergence. Let 
 $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f_n},c_n\lambda, \mathbf{p}_n)\in {\mathcal M}^{\rm doubl}_{D, \epsilon,\delta}$, with $c_n=\lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_{f_n}}(\mathbf{p}_n, 1))^{-1}$, and $\mathbf{p}_n\in {\mathbb R}^d$. By Lemma~\ref{lem: rescaling}, every sequence of spaces 
 \[
 ({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_{f_n},c_n\lambda,\mathbf{p}_n)
 \]
 is isomorphic to
 \[
 ({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_{g_n}, d_n\lambda, \mathbf{0}),
 \]
 for some $d_n>0$ and some $g_n\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ with $g_n(0)=0, \operatorname{osc}(g_n,[-1,1])=1$. Moreover, we have that $d_n=\lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_{g_n}}(\mathbf{0},1))^{-1}$, since the isomorphism preserves the volume of the unit ball. By Lemma \ref{lem:doublingpart}, the constants $d_n>0$ are bounded uniformly from above and below by positive and finite quantities. Thus, after passing to a subsequence, we infer that $d_n\to d$.

 By Lemma~\ref{lem:equicont}, the sequence $g_n:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ is precompact in the topology of locally uniform convergence. Up to passing to a subsequence, we may thus assume that $g_n$ converges locally uniformly to a continuous function $g\in \mathcal{F}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$ with $g(0)=0, \operatorname{osc}(g,[-1,1])=1$.  Now, the pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_{g_n}, d_n\lambda, \mathbf{0})\to ({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_{g}, d\lambda, \mathbf{0})$ follows from Lemma \ref{lem: convergence}. Finally, the correct normalization $d=\lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_{g}}(\mathbf{0},1))^{-1}$ follows since from vague convergence together with geodesicity implies $\lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_{g_n}}(\mathbf{0},1))\to \lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_{g}}(\mathbf{0},1))$. Here, we use the standard fact \cite[Corollary 2.2]{Buckley} that since $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_{g}, d\lambda, \mathbf{0})$ is geodesic and doubling $\lambda(\partial B_{\mathbf{d}_{g}}(\mathbf{0},1))=0$.

label: thm: Poincare
title: Theorem
body_md: \label{thm: Poincare} If $f\in C^0({\mathbb R})$ is a function that has doubling and reverse doubling oscillation, then $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_f,\lambda)$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality in the sense of \eqref{eq:PIineq}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:lanconelli} it suffices to construct for every ball $B(\mathbf{p},r)$ and sets $Q,\Omega$, and an almost exponential map $E$ that satisfies the assumptions. Note here that the triangle inequality then implies that the left-hand side in \eqref{eq:PIineq} is bounded from above by $\lambda(B)^{-2}$  times the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:weakPI}. The Poincar\'e inequality follows from this and doubling in Lemma \ref{lem:doublingpart}.

Assume that $f$ is a function that has doubling oscillation with constant $D$ and reverse doubling oscillation with constants $(\epsilon_f,\delta_f)\in (0,1)^2$. Fix $\delta \in (0,(4d)^{-1})$, with its precise value determined in the course of the proof. Let $r>0,\mathbf{p}\in {\mathbb R}^d$, $t_1,\dots, t_{d-1}\in [-r/(4d),r/(4d)]$ be such that $\{f(p_1+t_i):i=1,\dots, d-1\}$ is an equipartition of $f([p_1-r/(4d),p_1+r/(4d)]).$ For $\mathbf{q}=(q_1,\mathbf{q}_{-1})\in {\mathbb R}^d$ write $\mathbf{V}_\mathbf{q}:={\bf Van}(f(q_1+t_1), \dots, f(q_1+t_{d-1}))$ and $\Omega := B(\mathbf{p},\delta r)$, and $m_\mathbf{q}=\min_{i\neq j} |f(q_1+t_{i})-f(q_1+t_{j})|$. Let $\omega=\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r/(4d),p_1+r/(4d)])$.

We have $m_{\mathbf{p}}=\frac{\omega}{d-2}$. Choose $k_0\in {\mathbb N}$ such that  $D\epsilon_f^{k_0}\leq \frac{1}{4(d-2)}$ and assume that $\delta \leq \delta_f^{k_0}/(4d)$. For every $\mathbf{q}\in \Omega$ we have $|q_1-p_1|\leq \delta r$, and thus 
\begin{align*}
|f(p_1+t_i)-f(q_1+t_i)|&\leq \operatorname{osc}(f, [p_1+t_i-\delta r, p_1+t_i + \delta r]) \\
&\leq \epsilon_f^{k_0}\operatorname{osc}(f, [p_1+t_i-r/(4d), p_1+t_i + r/(4d)]) \\
&\leq \epsilon_f^{k_0}\operatorname{osc}(f, [p_1-r/(2d), p_1+ r/(2d)]) \\
&\leq D\epsilon_f^{k_0}\omega \leq \frac{\omega}{4(d-2)}.
\end{align*}
Using this, we get $m_{\mathbf{q}} \geq \frac{\omega}{4(d-2)}$. Also, let $M_{\mathbf{q}}=\max_{i}|f(q_1+t_i)-f(q_1)|\leq \operatorname{osc}(f,[q_1-r/(4d), q_1+r/(4d)])\leq \operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r/(2d), p_1+r/(2d)]) \leq D \omega$.


Define for $\mathbf{h}=(h_1,\mathbf{h}_{-1})\in {\mathbb R}^d$
\[
E(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}):=\mathbf{q} + (h_1, \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{h}_{-1}).
\]
Notice that $E$ is linear in $\mathbf{h}$, and thus $D(x,\cdot)=|\det(D_{\mathbf{h}}E(x,\cdot))|$ is constant. We thus obtain the conditions $(1)--(2)$ of an almost exponential map with $a=1$. Next, we verify controllability, and the remaining assumptions in Theorem \ref{thm:lanconelli}.

By the Ball-Box Theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm: ballbox}, with $\delta_2=\operatorname{osc}(f,[q_1-4r,q_1+4r])$ we have $\delta_2 \leq \operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-5r,p_1+5r]) \leq D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ballboxq}
B(\mathbf{p}, r)\subset B(\mathbf{q},2r)\subset \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{Box}(D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega, 4dr)).
\end{equation}
Let $E_\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{h})=E(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{h})$. We have $E_\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{q}}(h_1, \mathbf{h}_{-1})=(h_1, \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}\mathbf{L}^{-1}_{f(q_1)}\mathbf{h}_{-1})$. By Lemma~\ref{lem: approxinv}, 
\[
\mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}\mathbf{L}^{-1}_{f(q_1)}=\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{m_\mathbf{q}}^{-1}
\]
for a matrix $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}$ with 
\[
\|\mathbf{M}_\mathbf{q}^{-1}\|\leq (d-1)^{d-2}\max\left\{1,\frac{M_\mathbf{q}}{m_\mathbf{q}}\right\}^{(d-2)^2} \leq (d-1)^{d-2} (4(d-2)D)^{(d-2)^2}.
\]

\begin{align}
    E_\mathbf{q}^{-1}\mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{Box}(D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega, 4dr)) &\subset [-4dr,4dr]\times \mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{m_\mathbf{q}}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega}\left([- 4dr, 4dr]^{d-1}\right) \nonumber\\ 
    &\subset [-4dr,4dr]\times \mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega m_q^{-1}} \left([- 4dr, 4dr]^{d-1}\right) \nonumber\\ 
    &\subset [-4dr,4dr]\times \mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{4(d-2)D^{\log_2(d)+6}} \left([- 4dr, 4dr]^{d-1}\right), \nonumber \\
    &\subset [-4dr,4dr]\times [- C_{D,d}r, C_{D,d}r]^{d-1}, \label{eq:inclusionballs}
\end{align}
where on the last line we used 
\[
\|\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{4(d-2)D^{\log_2(d)+6}}\|_{\ell^\infty} \leq d\|\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1} \mathbf{D}_{4(d-2)D^{\log_2(d)+6}}\|\leq C_{D,d}/(4d)
\]
where $C_{D,d}$ is a sufficiently large constant and $\|\cdot\|_{\ell_\infty}$ is the operator norm with respect to the $\ell_\infty$-metric.

Let
\[
Q:=[-4dr,4dr]\times [- C_{D,d}r, C_{D,d}r]^{d-1}.
\]
From \eqref{eq:inclusionballs} and \eqref{eq:ballboxq}, we get

\[
B(\mathbf{p},r)\subset \mathbf{T}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{Box}(D^{\log_2(d)+6}\omega, 4dr)) \subset E(\mathbf{q},Q); \qquad \forall \mathbf{q}\in \Omega.
\]
                           
Next, after fixing $\mathbf{q}\in \Omega$, we consider the same points we did in \eqref{some points} with $y_i:=h_{i+1}$ and $\mathbf{p}_1:=\mathbf{q}$. However, we now parametrize the curves joining these points differently from the ${\boldsymbol{\gamma}}^i$ in \eqref{some curves}.
                                                                   
                                        
    
               
                  
                                                           
                                  
                                    
            
   
                                                                           
                                                                    
                                                                     
To simplify notation, let $R:=\max(C_{D,d}, 4d)r$. For $i\in\{1,\dots, d-1\}$ set
\[
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t):=\begin{cases} e^{\frac{t-3(i-1)R}{R} \cdot t_i\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{p}^i & \text{for } t\in [3(i-1)R, 3(i-1)R+R] \\
e^{\frac{t-3(i-1)R-R}{R} \cdot h_{i+1} \mathbf{Y}}e^{t_i\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{p}^i & \text{for } t\in [3(i-1)R+R, 3(i-1)R+2R]\\
e^{-\frac{t-3(i-1)R-2R}{R} \cdot t_i\mathbf{X}}e^{h_{i+1} \mathbf{Y}}e^{t_i\mathbf{X}}\mathbf{p}^i & \text{for } t\in [3(i-1)R+2R, 3iR].\end{cases}
\]
Also, define for $t\in [3(d-1)R,3dR]$
\[
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t):=e^{\frac{t-3(d-1)R}{3R} h_{1}\mathbf{X}} \mathbf{p}^{d}.
\]
Set $T:=3dR$. We have $E(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{h})=\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h},T)$ and $\boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h},0)=\mathbf{q}$. By a direct calculation we also have $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t)'=a(t) {\mathbf X} + b(t)\mathbf{Y}$ with $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\leq 1$ since $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t)$ is piecewise a constant multiple of $\mathbf{X}$ or $\mathbf{Y}$. The control function is now given by
\[
\gamma(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h},t)=\gamma_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t).
\]
Fix $t\in [0, T]$ and $\mathbf{h}\in Q$. A simple proof by induction on $i$ in the construction of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{h}}$ shows that for $\mathbf{q}=(q_1,\mathbf{q}_{-1})$ we have
\[
\gamma_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t)=(q_1+c_{t,\mathbf{h}}, \mathbf{q}_{-1}+H_{\mathbf{h}}(q_1,t))
\]
for some continuous $c_{t,\mathbf{h}}$ and $H_{\mathbf{h}}(q_1,t)$ which depends continuously on $q_1$. For every fixed $q_1$, this map is a translation that shifts the $x_1=q_1$ slice to $x_1=q_1+c_t$. This translation preserves the volume of the cross-section, and by Fubini, the map $\mathbf{q}\mapsto \gamma_{\mathbf{q},\mathbf{h}}(t)$ is volume-preserving. Thus, we can take $b=1$ in the definition of controllability. From this formula, it is also direct to see that this map is injective.

                                                                                                                                                                   
   
                                                             
   
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
   
                                  
   
                                                                                                                                           

Only the conditions (1) and (3) from Theorem~\ref{thm:lanconelli} remain to be checked. Both conditions follow since Lemma~\ref{lem:doublingpart} gives that $\lambda$ is doubling with respect to the metric $\mathbf{d}_f$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For $Q=\frac{d(d-1)+2}{2}$, one can use $f(x)=x$ and the space $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_f, \lambda, \mathbf{0})$ is the filiform Carnot group of the first type, which satisfies $(1)-(5)$ by classical results; see e.g. \cite{LeDonneGTM}. The claims on Ahlfors regularity and LLC, analytic dimension and the Poincar\'e inequality follow also from Lemma~\ref{lem:doublingpart},  Theorem~\ref{thm: analyticdim}, and Theorem~\ref{thm: Poincare} respectively. Carnot groups are homogeneous and admit scalings, and thus $\mathcal{F}=\{({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_f, \lambda/\lambda(B(\mathbf{0},1)), \mathbf{0})\}$ is invariant under scalings and changes of basepoints. This class is clearly compact with respect to pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence. 

For $Q\in (d,\frac{d(d-1)+2}{2})$ let $\alpha :=\frac{2(Q-d)}{(d-2)(d-1)} \in (0,1)$. Let $\mathcal{F}^{\rm reg}_{C, \alpha}$ be the non-empty collection of $\alpha$-regular functions from Lemma~\ref{lem: oscillationfunctions}. In this case, the class of spaces is $\mathcal{F}={\mathcal M}^{\rm reg}_{C,\alpha}$ as constructed in Section~\ref{sec: GH}. This is closed under pointed measured Gromov-Hausdorff convergence by Theorem~\ref{thm: closed}. The claims on Ahlfors regularity and LLC, analytic dimension and the Poincar\'e inequality follow again from Lemma~\ref{lem:doublingpart},  Theorem~\ref{thm: analyticdim}, and Theorem~\ref{thm: Poincare} respectively. The completeness, homeomorphism with ${\mathbb R}^d$ and geodesic properties follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $Q>\frac{d(d-1)+2}{2}$, one sets $\alpha :=\frac{2(Q-d)}{(d-2)(d-1)} >1$ and uses Lemma~\ref{lem: oscillationfunctions} to give a continuous monotone function $f$ of doubling oscillation for which 
\[
\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{\log(\operatorname{osc}(f,[p_1-r,p_1+r]))}{\log(r)}=\alpha, 
\]
for a.e. $p_1\in {\mathbb R}$. Any monotone function $f$ of doubling oscillation also has reverse doubling oscillation. This is seen as follows. Let $D>1$ be the constant of doubling oscillation. If $I\subset J$ is an interval of length at most half of $J$, then the closure of $J\setminus I$ contains an interval $K$ of length at least $1/4$ of the length of $J$. Since $f$ has doubling oscillation, we have $\operatorname{osc}(f,K)\geq D^{-3}\operatorname{osc}(f,J)$. Since $f$ is monotone, we have
$\operatorname{osc}(f,I)\leq \operatorname{osc}(f,J)-\operatorname{osc}(f,K) \leq (1-D^{-3})\operatorname{osc}(f,J)$. Thus, we get the reverse doubling oscillation property with $\epsilon=1-D^{-3}$and $\delta=1/2$.

Now, the measure doubling and LLC properties of $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_f, \lambda, \mathbf{0})$ follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:doublingpart}, the Poincar\'e inequality from Theorem~\ref{thm: Poincare} and the analytic dimension from Theorem~\ref{thm: analyticdim}. The completeness, homeomorphism with ${\mathbb R}^d$, and geodesic properties follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:boundedcompact}. The fact that every blow-up of $({\mathbb R}^d,\mathbf{d}_f)$ is homeomorphic to Euclidean space follows from Theorem~\ref{thm: closed}, since $({\mathbb R}^d, \mathbf{d}_f, \lambda/\lambda(B_{\mathbf{d}_f}(\mathbf{0},1)), \mathbf{0})\in \mathcal{M}^{\rm doubl}_{D,\epsilon,\delta}$, and the latter is closed under scalings, changes of basepoints, and Gromov-Hausdorff limits.

Finally, we show the claim on essential dimension. From the volume estimates in Lemma~\ref{lem:doublingpart} we get for Lebesgue a.e. $\mathbf{p}\in {\mathbb R}^d$ that
\[
\lim_{r\to 0} \frac{\log(\mu(B(\mathbf{p}, r)))}{\log(r)}=Q.
\]
That the essential dimension of $\mu$ is $Q$, and that every set of positive measure has Hausdorff dimension at least $Q$, now follow from this and Lemma~\ref{lem: billinglsey}.

label: lem:diffind
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:diffind}
A separable metric measure space  $(X,d,\mu)$ is a differentiability space with analytic dimension at most $N$ if and only if for every Lipschitz $F: X\to {\mathbb R}^M$ such that  $\mu({\rm Ind}(F))>0$ it holds $M\leq N$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The condition is sufficient for differentiability by \cite[Proposition~4.1]{KleinerMackay}, where \cite[Definition~2.3]{KleinerMackay} is equivalent to our condition on independence. Next, we show the necessity. Assume that $(X,\mathbf{d},\mu)$ is a differentiability space of analytic dimension $N$, and $F:X\to {\mathbb R}^M$ is such that  $\mu({\rm Ind}(F))>0$. It suffices to prove $M\leq N$. Assume not, i.e., $M>N$. Choose a chart $(U_i,\phi_i)$  with $\phi_i:X\to {\mathbb R}^{n_i}$, and $U_i\cap {\rm Ind}(F)$ having positive measure with $n_i\leq N<M$. Consider the differentials $df_{k,i}$ for $k=1,\dots, M$. Since $n_i<M$, for a.e. $p\in {\rm Ind}(F) \cap U_i$ there is some linear combination $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots, a_M)\in {\mathbb R}^M$ with $|\mathbf{a}|=1$ of these differentials that vanishes, i.e., $\sum_{k=1}^M a_k df_{k,i,p} = 0$. At these points
    \[
    \operatorname{Lip}\left[\sum_{k=1}^M a_k f_{k}\right](p) = \operatorname{Lip}\left[\sum_{k=1}^M a_k (f_{k}-df_{k,i,p}\circ \phi_i)\right](p)\stackrel{\eqref{eq:diff}}{=}0.
    \]
    This contradicts \eqref{d:indep} and thus we must have $M\leq N$.

label: lem:upperbound
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lem:upperbound} Assume that $(X,d,\mu)$ is a geodesic Lipschitz differentiability space and that $\Omega\subset X$ is a non-empty open set. If $F=(f_1,\dots, f_n):X \to {\mathbb R}^n$ is a Lipschitz map such that $F|_\Omega$ is a weakly $C$-BLD map and $\mu(\Omega\cap {\rm Ind}(F))>0$, then for any chart $(U_i,\phi_i)$ with $\phi_i:X\to {\mathbb R}^{n_i}$ of $X$ with $\mu(U_i\cap {\rm Ind}(F) \cap\Omega)>0$, we have $n_i= n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M\geq n$ be the maximal integer such that  we can add $1$-Lipschitz coordinates to $F$ in such a way that $\widetilde{F}=(f_1,\dots, f_M)$ is Lipschitz and $\mu(\Omega\cap {\rm Ind}(\widetilde{F})\cap U_i)$ has positive measure. By Lemma~\ref{lem:diffind} applied to the restricted metric measure space $(U_i, d|_{U_i}, \mu|_{U_i})$, or just \cite[Lemma 4.2]{KleinerMackay}, there is an upper bound for $M\leq n_i$ and such a maximal $M$ exists. Here, one also uses a well-known fact that Lipschitz differentiability implies that porous sets have measure zero \cite[Theorem 2.4]{BS}. This in turn implies that for any Lipschitz function $f:X\to{\mathbb R}$ and any measurable subset $U\subset X$, we have $\operatorname{Lip}[f|_U](x)=\operatorname{Lip}[f](x)$ for $\mu$-a.e. $x\in U$, and thus independence is preserved when passing to subsets.

    By the proof of \cite[Lemma 4.2]{KleinerMackay}, it follows that $({\rm Ind}(\widetilde{F})\cap \Omega\cap U_i, \widetilde{F})$ is a chart. We must have $n_i=M$, since charts are independent (since otherwise the differential is not unique) and we can apply the argument from the previous lemma. Thus, it suffices to prove that $M=n$. 
    
    Assume for the sake of contradiction that $M>n$. Let $\mathcal{C}=\{v=(v_1,\dots, v_M) : v_M > 2C\|(v_1,\dots, v_{M-1})\|>0\}$ be an open cone of vectors.
    By density of directions in charts \cite[Theorem 9.5.]{Bate} there exists a curve fragment $\gamma:K\to {\rm Ind}(\widetilde{F})\cap \Omega\cap U_i$ with $\lambda(K)>0$, $K\subset {\mathbb R}$ such that  for a.e. $t\in K$
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $t$ is a Lebesgue density point of $K$;
        \item $\widetilde{F}\circ \gamma$ is differentiable at $t$ and $(\widetilde{F}\circ \gamma)'(t)=\widetilde{w}(t)\in \mathcal{C}$
        \item $\gamma$ is metrically differentiable at $t$ and $|\dot\gamma|(t)>0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Let $w(t)=(F\circ\gamma)'(t)$ be the vector formed by the first $n$ components of $\widetilde{w}(t)$. Let $\sigma$ be the geodesic interpolation of $\gamma$. We have that $\sigma$ is metrically differentiable and $\widetilde{F}\circ \gamma$ is differentiable, whenever $t$ is as above. Moreover, since a subsequential limit equals the full limit, $|\dot\gamma|(t)=|\dot{\sigma}|(t)$ and $(\widetilde{F}\circ \gamma)'(t)=(\widetilde{F}\circ \sigma)'(t)$ for all such $t\in K$ where both limits exist.

    We have for a.e. $t\in K$ that $|\dot\gamma|(t)=|\dot{\sigma}|(t)\leq C|(F\circ \sigma)'(t)|=C|(F\circ \gamma)'(t)|=C\|w\|$ since $F|_\Omega$ is weakly BLD. Since $\widetilde{w}\in \mathcal{C}$, we also have $2C\|w\|\leq |\widetilde{w}_{M}|$. Finally, $|\widetilde{w}_{M}|\leq |\dot\gamma|(t)$ since $f_{M}$ is $1$-Lipschitz. By combining these we get
    \[
    0<|\dot\gamma|(t)\leq C\|w\|\leq |\widetilde{w}_{M}|/2\leq  |\dot\gamma|(t)/2, 
    \]
    for a.e. $t\in K$, which is a contradiction. Thus $M=n$.

label: thm: analyticdim
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: analyticdim} Let $({\mathbb R}^d, \Delta, \|\cdot\|)$ be a continuous Carnot-Carath\'eodory structure such that the space $({\mathbb R}^d,d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|})$ is boundedly compact and such that the topology generated by $d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|}$ is the same as the Euclidean topology, and let $\mu$ be a Radon measure on ${\mathbb R}^d$. If $({\mathbb R}^d, d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|}, \mu)$ is a differentiability space, then 
                          
its analytic dimension equals the rank of $\Delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $N$ be the rank of $\Delta$, i.e., the dimension of its fibers. 
   We may cover the space by open sets $\Omega$, such that some orthogonal projection onto an $N$-dimensional space is $L$-biLipschitz when restricted to $(\Delta_p, \|\cdot\|)$ for every $p\in \Omega$ for some $L>1$. Fix one such $\Omega$ and consider the orthogonal projection $\Pi|_{\Omega}$ onto the given subspace. Extend this by the McShane Theorem to a Lipschitz function on all of $({\mathbb R}^d,d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|})$, possibly increasing the Lipschitz constant by a constant.  To simplify notation, rotate so that the projection corresponds to the first $N$ coordinates, i.e., $\Pi=(\pi_1,\dots, \pi_N)$.
    
    First, we show that $\Pi$ is independent on $\Omega$, i.e., Equation \eqref{d:indep} holds almost everywhere with $F:=\Pi$. Up to biLipschitz equivalence, we may assume that the norm $\|\cdot\|$ comes from a scalar product, and so we choose a linearly independent set of continuous unit length vector fields $\mathbf{X}_1,\dots, \mathbf{X}_N$ in $\Omega$ that span $\Delta_p$, for each $p\in \Omega$. For each $k\in \{1,\dots, N\}$ and each $p\in \Omega$, by Peano's theorem, we can find a curve $\gamma_k:(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\to {\mathbb R}^d$ such that  $\gamma_k(0)=p$ and $ \dot\gamma_k(t)=\mathbf{X}_k(\gamma_k(t))$ for $t\in (-\epsilon,\epsilon)$. If $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots, a_N)\in {\mathbb R}^N$ is a vector, then we have by differentiation along each of these curves that
    \[
     \operatorname{Lip}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \pi_{i}\right](p) \geq \max_{k\in\{1,\dots, N\}}\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \mathbf{X}_{k,i}\right|\right).
    \]
    Here $\mathbf{X}_{k, i}$ denote the $i$-th components of $\mathbf{X}_k$ at the point $p$. Let $\mathbf{X}$ be the full rank matrix with entries $(\mathbf{X}_{k,i})_{k,i=1}^N$ evaluated at $p$ for $k\in\{1,\dots, N\}$. This matrix is full rank in $\Omega$ by our choice of the projection $\Pi$. Then, we get
    \[
    \operatorname{Lip}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N a_i \pi_{i}\right](p) \geq \frac{1}{N} \|\mathbf{X} \mathbf{a}\|,
    \]
    which yields immediately \eqref{d:indep}. This yields a lower bound $N$ for the analytic dimension by Lemma~\ref{lem:diffind}.
    
     Next, we proceed to show the upper bound. For this, it suffices to prove that $\Pi$ is weakly $L$-BLD on $\Omega$, since then the claim follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:upperbound} by covering the space ${\mathbb R}^d$ by a countable collection of open sets as in the beginning of the proof. The $L$-BLD property follows from Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability} and its proof as follows. First, if $\gamma:[a,b]\to (\Omega, d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|}),$ is a Lipschitz curve, then Theorem~\ref{d_X rectifiability} shows that $\gamma$ is $\Delta$-horizontal and the length functionals agree, that is for all $t\in [a,b]$ we have
     \[
     \mathbf{L}_{\|\cdot \|}(\gamma|_{[a,t]})=\mathbf{L}_{d_{\Delta, \|\cdot\|}}(\gamma|_{[a,t]}).
     \]
     The derivative of the length functional gives the metric derivative for a.e. $t\in [a,b]$ by \cite[Theorem~2.7.6]{bbi}. Thus, differentiating these with respect to $t$, we get
     \[
     |\dot \gamma|(t)=\|\dot\gamma(t)\| \ \  \text{ for a.e.} \ \ t\in [a,b].
     \]
     By the assumption that $\Pi$ is $L$-biLipschitz when restricted to $\Delta_p$ for $p\in \Omega$, we get $\|\dot\gamma(t)\|\leq L |(\Pi\circ \gamma)'(t)|$ and thus $\Pi$ is $L$-BLD.
